subject: Parameters in MIRT versus Simulated Parameters

messages.author: b02cc32c527f7c33
messages.subject: Parameters in MIRT versus Simulated Parameters
parts:
Hello,

 

A little story time. A few days ago I was building an IRT demonstration using MIRT and I wanted to demonstrate how some specific item parameters function so I generated item parameters and responses using Wingen3. When I estimated the item parameters from the simulated responses I noticed there were a couple of oddly high a1 parameter estimates for a couple of items. I thought this was a little strange so I did a quick little simulation looking at a number of 50 item tests taken by 500, 1000, 2000, and 5000 respondents (100 replications per cell) with dichotomous responses scored through the 3PL to see how well MIRT was recovering parameters. I was a little surprised at what resulted. 

 

From a correlation standpoint MIRT performs quite well with recovery in the .8-.98 range. However, more surprising to me was when I looked at the deviation between estimated and simulated parameters there is a huge difference in a parameters. On average in each 50 item set a number of items have an a parameter 1 full point higher and a few items with an a parameter 2 points higher. It works out to be 99% of tests are affected by this with 500 responses or less and 74% of tests with 1000 responses. Even with 2000 responses 38% of tests had at least 1 a parameter having a difference of 1 and 12% having a difference of 2. The d and g parameters do not usually exhibit deviations more than 1 point higher.

What is causing this odd behavior? I spot checked the responses being generated with WinGen3 in MULTILOG and got very similar responses to the simulated results so I don’t believe it’s an issue with how WinGen3 is simulation responses.

Scott

On Thu, Sep 3, 2015 at 4:39 AM, Scott Withrow <swit...@ku.edu.tr> wrote:
I can attempt to replicate the issue with simdata. I thought about that first but I wasn't sure how simdata constructed response sets and I couldn't be sure that the problem wouldn't be hidden by conducting the entire simulation with MIRT.

It shouldn't really make much difference what generator is used to make response data. It really is just a matter of constructing expected probability functions and sampling across all possible values weighted by that probability. Just think sample(0:1, 1, prob = c(p0, p1)) repeated for each NxJ element. 

simdata() is really just a wrapper to create the internal IRT models defined in mirt, which are then used to generate the expected trace-lines, but of course one could do all this manually (and sometimes you should). In the current dev version you can pass whole mirt objects to the function, so helper functions like mirtCAT::generate.mirt_object are now much more useful, and the whole process seems that much more intuitive.

In the meantime here are all the files and syntax I used before if you feel like looking through them (https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/510411/MIRTEstTest.7z). WinGen3 is a pretty great item and response set generator available for free (you can Google it if you want to see it's documentation).

Perhaps so, but I have trouble investing in such programs, especially if you are familiar with R (and it looks like WinGen is by the very definition for Windows only, which is another negative for me because I run Linux and Mac OSX). All IRT models can easily be generated and sampled from with a bit of programming, including those not internally defined by the software (in some examples I show how to generate atypical models for item misfit detection reasons, and for generating polynomial latent trait effects. In WinGen and other stand-alone software, I'm not even sure if such things are possible). 

Food for thought of course; use whatever software is easiest, most comfortable, and suits the end-goal best. Cheers.

Phil

Best,
Scott

Hi Phil,

I understand completely trying to move away from a Windows ecosystem. Switching to Linux is actually why I moved away from software like IRTPRO to using R and packages like MIRT. It's been really beneficial for a lot of reasons. Of course I ended up at an organization that won't support anything other than a Windows computer.

I went ahead and conducted the same simulation I mentioned before this time I used sim.irt from the psych package to generate items. I still believe using a program to validate that same program is a bit circular but I might have this simulation run overnight too with simdata to see if the problem is still happening. With the psych package simulation function I got very similar results to the WinGen3 based item and response simulations. This time I made a few graphics as well to help show what it happening.

500 responses, 50 item tests, 100 cells

Median 12 6 2 1 0 0

Here we can see the same pattern of responses as before. This time it actually worked out to be much worse that the previous simulation where at least 6 items per test had an a parameter deviation of 1 point and all tests had at least 1 a parameter deviation of 2 points. The average number of deviations 1 or greater was 12 with 100% of tests being affected. The number of items exhibiting this difference decline as responses are added to the simulation.


For example, with 2000 responses:

Parameter recovery becomes much better and the average number of items exhibiting the a parameter errors drops to 4 but we still have 100% of tests having at least 1 a parameter deviating by 1 or more points.

With 5000 responses things are even better. However, from a practical standpoint many people will be using MIRT with less than 500 people.

Mean 1.37 0.31 0.33 0.24 0 0

Here is a sample of the syntax used:
# Scott Withrow
# 2015-09-03

#Testing MIRT's Estimation

require(mirt)
require(psych)

# Set working directory
setwd("E:/MIRTEstTest/5000/")

# Initialize variables
recovery.cor <- data.frame(NA)
difference <- matrix(NA, ncol = 6, nrow = 100)
nresponses <- 5000

for (i in 1:100){
  # Simulate item parameters and response vectors
  sim_data <- sim.irt(nvar = 50, n = nresponses, 
                      a = runif(50, 1, 4), 
                      d = runif(50, -3, 3),
                      c = runif(50, 0, .3),
                      mu = 0, sd = 1)
  
  # Check the simulated responses to make sure all items have
  # used all response categories or generate a new simulated set
  catcheck <- max(apply(sim_data$items, 2, function(x) length(which(x == 1))))
  
  while(catcheck == nresponses) {
    sim_data <- sim.irt(nvar = 50, n = nresponses, 
                        a = runif(50, 1, 4), 
                        d = runif(50, -3, 3),
                        c = runif(50, 0, .3),
                        mu = 0, sd = 1)
    
    catcheck <- max(apply(sim_data$items, 2, function(x) length(which(x == 1))))
  }
  
  # Extract response vectors
  irtdata <- sim_data$items
  
  # Extract item properties and save to data frame
  simparams <- data.frame(a1 = sim_data$discrimination,
                          d = sim_data$difficulty,
                          g = sim_data$gamma)
  
  # Save response vectors and item properties for repeatability of
  # simulation
  write.csv(irtdata, file = paste("itr", i, "responses.csv", sep = ""))
  write.csv(simparams, file = paste("itr", i, "parameters.csv", sep = ""))
  
  # Run the model
  model1 <- mirt(data = irtdata, 1, itemtype = "3PL", SE = FALSE,
                 technical = list(NCYCLES = 1500))
  
  # Extract the parameters
  model1.param <- coef(model1, as.data.frame = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)
  
  # Create a dataframe with just the parameters.
  estparam <- data.frame(a1 = model1.param[grepl("*a1", rownames(model1.param)), "par"],
                         d = model1.param[grepl("*d", rownames(model1.param)), "par"],
                         g = model1.param[grepl("*g", rownames(model1.param)), "par"])

  # Compare simulated vs estimated parameters
  recovery.a <- estparam["a1"]
  recovery.a[, 2] <- simparams["a1"]

  recovery.d <- -estparam["d"] / estparam["a1"]
  recovery.d[, 2] <- simparams["d"]

  recovery.g <- estparam["g"]
  recovery.g[, 2] <- simparams["g"]

messages.subject: Re: Parameters in MIRT versus Simulated Parameters
parts:
Hi Scott,

Okay I see the issue now, and it's actually been known for quite some time in the IRT literature. The problem is that estimating 3PL models via ML is notoriously difficult because the g parameter causes a lot of instability during estimation (often is collinear with the intercept if the item is too easy). ML estimation of 3PL models requires huge samples sizes, which your simulation also appears to be confirming.

One way people tend to get around this issue is to place prior parameter distributions on the estimates to help keep them more stable during estimation. Naturally, this means you are no longer estimation an ML solution but rather a MAP, but the bias introduced is generally thought to be a preventative measure and therefore necessary. I recommend using a normal prior (because of the internal reparameterizations this is the most optimal and intuitive) with a fairly tight SD. Something like this:

###
qlogis(.2) #logit mean
model <- 'F = 1-20
               PRIOR = (1-20, g, norm, -1.38, .5)' 
mod <- mirt(dat, model, itemtype = '3PL')
###

HTH.

Phil
On Thu, Sep 3, 2015 at 10:38 AM, Scott Withrow <swit...@ku.edu.tr> wrote:

Hi Phil,

I understand completely trying to move away from a Windows ecosystem. Switching to Linux is actually why I moved away from software like IRTPRO to using R and packages like MIRT. It's been really beneficial for a lot of reasons. Of course I ended up at an organization that won't support anything other than a Windows computer.

I went ahead and conducted the same simulation I mentioned before this time I used sim.irt from the psych package to generate items. I still believe using a program to validate that same program is a bit circular but I might have this simulation run overnight too with simdata to see if the problem is still happening. With the psych package simulation function I got very similar results to the WinGen3 based item and response simulations. This time I made a few graphics as well to help show what it happening.

# Scott Withrow
# 2015-09-03

#Testing MIRT's Estimation

require(mirt)
require(psych)

# Set working directory
setwd("E:/MIRTEstTest/5000/")

# Initialize variables
recovery.cor <- data.frame(NA)
difference <- matrix(NA, ncol = 6, nrow = 100)
nresponses <- 5000

for (i in 1:100){
  # Simulate item parameters and response vectors
  sim_data <- sim.irt(nvar = 50, n = nresponses, 
                      a = runif(50, 1, 4), 
                      d = runif(50, -3, 3),
                      c = runif(50, 0, .3),
                      mu = 0, sd = 1)
  
  # Check the simulated responses to make sure all items have
  # used all response categories or generate a new simulated set
  catcheck <- max(apply(sim_data$items, 2, function(x) length(which(x == 1))))
  
  while(catcheck == nresponses) {
    sim_data <- sim.irt(nvar = 50, n = nresponses, 
                        a = runif(50, 1, 4), 
                        d = runif(50, -3, 3),
                        c = runif(50, 0, .3),
                        mu = 0, sd = 1)
    
    catcheck <- max(apply(sim_data$items, 2, function(x) length(which(x == 1))))
  }
  
  # Extract response vectors
  irtdata <- sim_data$items
  
  # Extract item properties and save to data frame
  simparams <- data.frame(a1 = sim_data$discrimination,
                          d = sim_data$difficulty,
                          g = sim_data$gamma)
  
  # Save response vectors and item properties for repeatability of
  # simulation
  write.csv(irtdata, file = paste("itr", i, "responses.csv", sep = ""))
  write.csv(simparams, file = paste("itr", i, "parameters.csv", sep = ""))
  
  # Run the model
  model1 <- mirt(data = irtdata, 1, itemtype = "3PL", SE = FALSE,
                 technical = list(NCYCLES = 1500))
  
  # Extract the parameters
  model1.param <- coef(model1, as.data.frame = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)
  
  # Create a dataframe with just the parameters.
  estparam <- data.frame(a1 = model1.param[grepl("*a1", rownames(model1.param)), "par"],
                         d = model1.param[grepl("*d", rownames(model1.param)), "par"],
                         g = model1.param[grepl("*g", rownames(model1.param)), "par"])

  # Compare simulated vs estimated parameters
  recovery.a <- estparam["a1"]
  recovery.a[, 2] <- simparams["a1"]

  recovery.d <- -estparam["d"] / estparam["a1"]
  recovery.d[, 2] <- simparams["d"]

  recovery.g <- estparam["g"]
  recovery.g[, 2] <- simparams["g"]

  # Calculate the correlation between estimated and simulated parameters.
  recovery.cor[i, 1] <- data.frame(cor(recovery.a)[2])
  recovery.cor[i, 2] <- cor(recovery.d)[2]
  recovery.cor[i, 3] <- cor(recovery.g)[2]

  # Difference
  dif.a <- recovery.a[,1] - recovery.a[, 2]
  dif.d <- recovery.d[,1] - recovery.d[, 2]
  dif.g <- recovery.g[,1] - recovery.g[, 2]
  
  # Note differences greater than 1 SD and 2 SD from simulated parameters.
  difference[i, ] <- matrix(c(length(dif.a[dif.a > 1 | dif.a < -1]),
                             length(dif.a[dif.a > 2 | dif.a < -2]),
                             length(dif.d[dif.d > 1 | dif.d < -1]),
                             length(dif.d[dif.d > 2 | dif.d < -2]),
                             length(dif.g[dif.g > 1 | dif.g < -1]),
                             length(dif.g[dif.g > 2 | dif.g < -2])),
                            byrow = FALSE)
  
  print(paste("Iteration", i, "completed"))
}
